The canonical record accidentally concatenates all of Problem 22 with the beginning of Problem 23.  The official AIM PDF shows that the part assigned here is Problem 22 and ends after the ridge-function question.  In the PDF, a comma is also missing between the displayed vectors $v_3$ and $v_4$, and OCR has inserted a comma into the sum $f_1+\cdots+f_n$.  With those typographical repairs, the recovered problem is:

> A measurable function $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ is a ridge function if
> $f(x)=g(\langle x,v\rangle)$ for a measurable $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and a direction $v$.  A superlevel set of a sum of ridge functions is uniquely determined among measurable sets by the corresponding X-rays.  The four directions
> \[
> v_1=(1,0),\qquad v_2=(0,1),\qquad v_3=(2,1),\qquad v_4=(-1,2)
> \]
> determine every planar convex body by X-rays, whereas three directions never suffice universally.  Is every planar convex body $K$ representable as
> \[
> K=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\sum_{i=1}^4 f_i(x)\geq 0\right\},
> \qquad f_i(x)=g_i(\langle x,v_i\rangle)?
> \]

The PDF writes $v\in S^1$, while $v_3,v_4$ are not unit vectors.  This is harmless: replacing $v$ by $cv$, $c\ne0$, only reparametrizes the univariate profile.

The text beginning “For $t>0$, $a\in S^{n-1}$, consider the slab” belongs to Problem 23, not Problem 22.  In particular, the canonical record stops at “on the right for $a=f$”; the official continuation is $f_2$, followed by the complex case and separate questions.  None of Problem 23 is analyzed here.
status_literature:
Fishburn--Lagarias--Reeds--Shepp proved the foundational implication “additive (ridge-threshold) set implies X-ray uniqueness” for coordinate projections.  Gardner developed the invariant formulation for arbitrary finite families of X-ray subspaces, proved that inscribable convex sets are additive, and showed that additivity is a genuinely stronger structure than mere uniqueness in the relevant general settings.  His 2006 book treats ridge functions and the additivity conjecture in Chapter 2, Section 2.6.  Dulio--Peri's later account again separates X-ray uniqueness, additivity, and inscribability.

This distinction is decisive: the premise that the displayed four X-rays determine every convex body **among convex bodies** does not supply ridge profiles, and a ridge-threshold body would be determined **among all measurable competitors** (modulo the usual null-set convention).  Thus one cannot infer the requested representation from the quoted four-direction uniqueness theorem.

Searches in July--August 2026 used the exact wording of the question, the exact direction tuple, the names Daurat and Gardner, and combinations of “ridge functions,” “additive,” “convex body,” and “X-rays.”  They located the AIM list and the general sources above, but no primary paper claiming a resolution of this exact universal four-direction question.  Accordingly it is treated as apparently open in the literature checked, not as proved open by an exhaustive bibliography search.

There are two conventions to keep separate.  Classical X-rays only see sets modulo planar null sets, and Gardner's formulation uses equality modulo null sets.  The AIM display literally asks for the closed convex body $K=\{F\ge0\}$.  The positive constructions below satisfy literal equality, including the boundary.  The finite switching obstruction below is also pointwise and therefore does not, by itself, obstruct a representation after arbitrary null-set changes.

### 3. Definitions and assumptions

Put
\[
 \ell_1(x,y)=x,\quad \ell_2(x,y)=y,\quad
 \ell_3(x,y)=2x+y,\quad \ell_4(x,y)=-x+2y.
\]
A four-ridge score is
\[
 F(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^4 g_i(\ell_i(x,y)),
\]
where each $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is measurable and finite valued.  Literal representability means $K=\{F\ge0\}$; in particular, $F<0$ at every point outside $K$.

For the obstruction, a finite signed configuration is a finitely supported function $c:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$.  It has zero $\ell_i$-marginal when
\[
 \sum_{p:\,\ell_i(p)=t}c(p)=0
 \quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.
\]
Only finitely many of these sums are nonempty.

### 4. Approach map

Three complementary routes were pursued.

1. **Algebraic positive classes.**  Determine exactly which low-degree polynomial scores are generated by the four fixed ridge directions.  This gives explicit representations of every ellipse.
2. **Geometric positive classes.**  Use discontinuous profiles to encode intersections of strips whose normals are among the four $v_i$.
3. **Dual obstruction.**  Derive finite signed configurations annihilating every possible four-ridge score, without imposing continuity, differentiability, or boundedness on the profiles.

The first two yield rigorous special cases.  The third gives a falsifiable route to a counterexample, but no sign-separated configuration for a convex body was found; hence the universal question remains unresolved.

### 7. Detailed proof, derivation, or heuristic

#### Proof of Theorem 5.1

Let $\mathcal H_k$ be the vector space of homogeneous binary forms of degree $k$, so $\dim\mathcal H_k=k+1$.

For $k=1$, $\ell_1=x$ and $\ell_2=y$ form a basis.  For $k=2$,
\[
 \ell_1^2=x^2,\qquad \ell_2^2=y^2,\qquad
 \ell_3^2=4x^2+4xy+y^2,
\]
so $\ell_1^2,\ell_2^2,\ell_3^2$ span all of $\mathcal H_2$.

For $k=3$, the pure terms are supplied by $\ell_1^3=x^3$ and $\ell_2^3=y^3$.  The other two cubes are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \ell_3^3&=8x^3+12x^2y+6xy^2+y^3,\\
 \ell_4^3&=-x^3+6x^2y-12xy^2+8y^3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Their coefficient matrix on the two mixed monomials $(x^2y,xy^2)$ is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}12&6\\6&-12\end{pmatrix},
\]
whose determinant is $-180\ne0$.  Hence the four cubes span $\mathcal H_3$.

Decompose any $P$ of degree at most three into homogeneous components.  Express its degree-$k$ component as a linear combination of the displayed $k$-th powers, and collect, for each $i$, all coefficients multiplying $\ell_i^k$ into a single univariate polynomial $G_i$.  This proves the cubic assertion.  Omitting the $k=3$ step shows that three directions suffice through degree two.

For reference, if a homogeneous cubic is
\[
 A x^3+B x^2y+Cxy^2+D y^3,
\]
the coefficients of $\ell_3^3$ and $\ell_4^3$ can be chosen as
\[
 r_3=\frac{2B+C}{30},\qquad r_4=\frac{B-2C}{30},
\]
after which the $\ell_1^3,\ell_2^3$ coefficients correct the pure terms.  This makes the spanning proof constructive.

#### Proof of Corollary 5.2

Substitution gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g_1(x)+g_2(y)+g_3(2x+y)
 &=(-a+2b)x^2+\alpha x+c+(-d+b/2)y^2+\beta y\\
 &\quad -(b/2)(4x^2+4xy+y^2)\\
 &=c+\alpha x+\beta y-a x^2-2bxy-dy^2=q(x,y).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore their nonnegative superlevel sets agree pointwise.

#### Proof of Proposition 5.3

Define
\[
 g_i(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\in I_i,\\-1,&t\notin I_i.\end{cases}
\]
If $x\in K$, every summand is zero.  If $x\notin K$, at least one summand is $-1$ and none is positive, so the sum is negative.  Hence $K=\{\sum_i g_i(\ell_i)\ge0\}$ exactly.  A polygon with the stated facet normals is the intersection of upper and lower bounds on the corresponding $\ell_i$, which combine into intervals $I_i$.

#### Proof of Proposition 5.4

For any ridge score $F=\sum_i g_i\circ\ell_i$, finiteness of the support permits regrouping:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_p c(p)F(p)
 &=\sum_{i=1}^4\sum_p c(p)g_i(\ell_i(p))\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^4\sum_t g_i(t)
   \left(\sum_{p:\ell_i(p)=t}c(p)\right)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Suppose, for example, $c>0$ only on $K$ and $c<0$ only outside $K$.  Literal equality $K=\{F\ge0\}$ makes every summand $c(p)F(p)$ nonnegative, and every outside summand strictly positive because both factors are negative.  A nonzero zero-marginal configuration has both signs (indeed $\sum_p c(p)=0$), so the total is strictly positive, contradicting the displayed identity.  Reversing signs yields the analogous strictly negative contradiction.

For the explicit configuration, pair in the sum the terms with $\varepsilon_i=0$ and $\varepsilon_i=1$.  The two points differ by $w_i\in\ker\ell_i$, so they have the same $\ell_i$-value and opposite coefficients.  Thus every $\ell_i$-marginal vanishes.  The same proof works with $w_i$ replaced by any nonzero scalar multiple.

### 8. Verification and attempted falsification

- The official PDF was checked directly.  It confirms the Problem 22 endpoint, all four vectors, the intended sum, and that the following slab material belongs to Problem 23.
- The cubic spanning determinant is $-180$, so no hidden linear dependence occurs in degree three.
- Direct expansion of the ellipsoid formula recovers the $x^2$, $xy$, $y^2$, linear, and constant coefficients exactly.
- The strip construction was checked on boundary points: closed interval endpoints give score $0$, so the requested $\ge0$ convention includes them.
- The switching proof uses only finite sums and finite-valued evaluations; it does not smuggle in continuity or integrability assumptions.
- Coincident atoms in the 16-term configuration do not invalidate marginal cancellation; they are combined algebraically before the sign test.
- The strongest tempting but invalid inference was explicitly rejected: uniqueness among convex bodies from four X-rays does not imply additivity or uniqueness among all measurable sets.
- No attempt was made to claim that every smooth convex body has a polynomial defining score.  Approximating a body by representable polynomials or strip polygons would not give an exact representation because additivity need not be closed under the relevant limit.
result:
### 5. Main result

#### Theorem 5.1 (polynomial completeness through degree three)

For the four linear forms $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_4$, every polynomial $P\in\mathbb R[x,y]$ of total degree at most three can be written
\[
 P(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^4 G_i(\ell_i(x,y))
\]
with univariate polynomials $G_i\in\mathbb R[t]$ of degree at most three.  Every polynomial of degree at most two can be represented using only $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$.

#### Corollary 5.2 (all ellipses, exactly, with three ridges)

Let
\[
 q(x,y)=c+\alpha x+\beta y-a x^2-2bxy-dy^2,
 \qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}>0.
\]
Whenever $K=\{q\ge0\}$ is nonempty, it is an ellipse (possibly with the usual degenerate limiting cases if positive definiteness is relaxed), and the exact representation $K=\{g_1(\ell_1)+g_2(\ell_2)+g_3(\ell_3)+g_4(\ell_4)\ge0\}$ is obtained from
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g_1(t)&=(-a+2b)t^2+\alpha t+c,\\
 g_2(t)&=(-d+b/2)t^2+\beta t,\\
 g_3(t)&=-(b/2)t^2,\\
 g_4(t)&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
These profiles are continuous, and equality includes the ellipse boundary.

#### Proposition 5.3 (four-normal strip polygons)

For arbitrary intervals $I_i\subseteq\mathbb R$, allowing rays and all of $\mathbb R$, the set
\[
 K=\bigcap_{i=1}^4\ell_i^{-1}(I_i)
\]
has an exact four-ridge threshold representation.  Consequently, every convex polygon all of whose facet normals belong to the set of signed normals displayed above is representable.

#### Proposition 5.4 (finite switching certificate)

Let $c$ be a nonzero finite signed configuration having zero $\ell_i$-marginal for every $i=1,\ldots,4$.  If either
\[
 \{c>0\}\subset K,\quad \{c<0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\setminus K,
\]
or the same inclusions with the two signs reversed, then no measurable finite-valued profiles $g_i$ can satisfy the literal equality
\[
 K=\left\{\sum_i g_i\circ\ell_i\ge0\right\}.
\]

There is an explicit family of such zero-marginal configurations.  Choose
\[
 w_1=(0,1),\quad w_2=(1,0),\quad w_3=(1,-2),\quad w_4=(2,1),
\]
so that $\ell_i(w_i)=0$.  For any base point $z$, define
\[
 \mu_z=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^4}
 (-1)^{|\varepsilon|}\,
 \delta_{z+\varepsilon_1w_1+\cdots+\varepsilon_4w_4}.
\]
This signed measure is nonzero even after coincident atoms are combined.  Indeed, in the group ring of the finitely generated torsion-free abelian group generated by the $w_i$, it is the translate of the product $\prod_i(1-X^{w_i})$.  That group ring is an integral domain and every factor is nonzero.  Its coefficient function has all four zero marginals.  Thus any translate and independently rescaled version whose positive and negative atoms are separated by membership in a convex $K$ would be a concrete counterexample certificate for the literal AIM formulation.

### 6. Candidate novel contribution

**Candidate claim.**  For the exact AIM direction tuple, every bivariate polynomial of degree at most three is a sum of four univariate ridge polynomials, and every quadratic uses only the first three directions; in particular, the displayed formula represents every planar ellipse exactly with three continuous ridge functions.

**Scope.**  This is a proved direction-specific special case.  It says nothing by itself about a general nonalgebraic convex boundary, nor does polynomial score completeness extend automatically to degree four or to arbitrary measurable scores.

**Why it may be new.**  Gardner's 1992 paper records strong uniqueness and additivity results, including an ellipsoid uniqueness theorem, but the exact low-degree spanning statement and the explicit formula for this AIM tuple were not found in the sources or exact-tuple searches.  The argument is elementary enough that it may well be folklore or implicit in ridge-function theory.

**Literature checked.**  The AIM problem list; Fishburn--Lagarias--Reeds--Shepp (1990); Gardner (1992); Gardner's 2006 monograph, especially Chapter 2; Dulio--Peri (2011); and exact web searches described in Section 2.

**Novelty confidence:** low.
what_remains:
### 9. Limitations and unresolved gaps

1. The universal question is not solved.  The positive classes (quadratic thresholds and four-normal strip intersections) are far smaller than all convex bodies.
2. The signed switching proposition is a criterion, not a counterexample: no choice of base point and kernel steps was proved to have one sign entirely in a convex body and the other entirely outside.
3. The finite certificate addresses the literal pointwise formulation.  Since finite sets are null, it is not an obstruction to equality modulo null sets.  A robust a.e. version would require a thickened zero-marginal signed measure and suitable boundedness or local integrability of the ridge profiles.
4. The degree-three theorem concerns equality of scores.  A body could have a ridge-threshold representation without possessing any polynomial ridge score, so a score-space dimension count in degree four cannot disprove threshold representability.
5. The current-status search was broad but not exhaustive; absence of a later exact-title hit is not proof that no unpublished or differently phrased resolution exists.

### 10. Concrete next steps

1. Study the parameterized switching family
   \(
   \prod_{i=1}^4(\delta_0-\delta_{s_iw_i})*\delta_z
   \)
   geometrically.  Either find a convex body separating its signed support, which would refute literal universality, or prove such separation impossible for this minimal family.
2. Replace atoms by compactly supported densities and formulate a bounded-profile, modulo-null dual certificate.  A rigorous infinite-dimensional separation theorem should identify whether all obstructions arise as limits of such switching measures.
3. Test structurally richer exact classes: bodies whose defining functions solve the ridge annihilation equation
   \(
   D_{w_1}D_{w_2}D_{w_3}D_{w_4}F=0
   \)
   under a nonvanishing-gradient boundary condition.  This PDE is necessary for $C^4$ ridge scores and may turn boundary geometry into explicit constraints.
4. Clarify whether the four-direction uniqueness proof supplies an inscribed-polygon mechanism for a substantial subclass of convex bodies; Gardner's theorem would then convert that geometric property into additivity.

### References

1. AIM, *Problems from the workshop Fourier analytic methods in convex geometry*, Problem 22, https://aimath.org/WWN/fourierconvex/fourierconvex.pdf.
2. P. C. Fishburn, J. C. Lagarias, J. A. Reeds, and L. A. Shepp, “Sets uniquely determined by projections on axes I. Continuous case,” *SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics* **50** (1990), 288--306, https://doi.org/10.1137/0150017.
3. R. J. Gardner, “Sets determined by finitely many X-rays,” *Geometriae Dedicata* **43** (1992), 1--16.
4. R. J. Gardner, *Geometric Tomography*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press, 2006, Chapter 2, especially Section 2.6, https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781107341029.005.
5. P. Dulio and C. Peri, “Intersecting polytopes and tomographic reconstructions,” Politecnico di Milano QDD 108 (2011), https://www.mate.polimi.it/biblioteca/add/quaderni/qdd108.pdf.
